section.name: BreakTest Features And Differences
section.p: This is the BreakTest manual. It documents the features and behavioral changes that are specific to BreakTest 2026.10.21. For the inherited JMeter-compatible test-plan model, use the official Apache JMeter documentation.

ul.li: Java 21 or later is required. HTTP/3 requires Java 27 or later; on older runtimes, explicit HTTP/3 requests fall back to HTTP/2 negotiation with a warning.
Virtual threads are used where they reduce thread overhead.
Legacy BeanShell, BSF/JEXL2, Rhino JavaScript, and LogKit paths were removed from the modern scripting/runtime surface.
JMeter-compatible names are retained where they are part of file formats, APIs, plugins, scripts, or automation.

section.p: Default contains the URL, parameters, body and headers. Protocol & Connections groups the wire protocol, HTTP/1.1 keep-alive and pool limits, timeouts, and source address. Proxy contains the proxy endpoint, credentials and destination host filters. Advanced contains embedded-resource downloads and response processing.

Keep-alive can be Not set, Enabled, Disabled, or an expression. Not set leaves the property absent; Disabled closes the HTTP/1.1 connection after the response, even if a custom Connection header requests keep-alive. The current request may still borrow an already-idle connection; it is not returned to the idle pool afterwards. As with other defaults, explicit sampler settings take precedence. Existing configurations are not changed on opening. The sampler's Browser-compatible multipart option affects only multipart form uploads: multipart part headers and their encoding. It does not emulate browser headers or browser execution. Redirect handling and multipart body options remain on individual samplers.

With a blank HTTP protocol on Java 27 or later, HTTPS requests start over TCP and negotiate HTTP/2 through TLS ALPN, falling back to HTTP/1.1. A same-host, same-port Alt-Svc advertisement enables HTTP/3 for subsequent requests through the same virtual user's client, including parallel requests. Without an advertisement, requests continue over TCP. Explicit HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 selections never upgrade. Each virtual user maintains its own discovery state. TCP connect time includes connection establishment and the TLS handshake; reused TCP connections report zero. The automatic path currently accepts alternatives at the original host and port only. Advertisements for another host or port stay on TCP because the JDK direct-HTTP/3 API cannot preserve the original authority while routing to another endpoint. Expired or cleared advertisements return subsequent requests to TCP. A failed HTTP/3 sample clears discovery for the next request without replaying that sample.

New HTTP Request Defaults enable Upgrade to HTTP/3 when advertised under Protocol & Connections for Automatic protocol selection. The saved checkbox overrides legacy global preferences. Unchecking it keeps all requests on HC5 TCP, even after another sampler has discovered HTTP/3. Explicit HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 ignore the checkbox. New explicit HTTP/3 profiles are HTTP/3-only on Java 27+; older runtimes fall back to HTTP/2 negotiation with a warning. Existing scripts keep absent settings absent when edited. They retain httpsampler.http3.prefer_for_default and the older-runtime fallback. The deprecated httpsampler.http3.force_http3=false now selects HC5 Automatic negotiation with Alt-Svc upgrade for legacy scripts, instead of JDK TCP fallback. All HTTP/2 requests use HC5. Older runtimes, multipart uploads, proxies and SSE use HttpClient5's HTTP/2-or-HTTP/1.1 path. HTTP/3 remains a beta transport.

Connect time is empty when no connection was established for the request (reuse), or when the transport cannot measure setup time (currently JDK HTTP/3). Only actual measurements contribute to connection-time averages. A genuinely measured zero milliseconds remains a numeric zero. CSV results use an empty Connect field; XML results omit the connect-time attribute. Older numeric values, including zero, remain readable without reinterpretation. The Java API retains a negative sentinel for missing values for compatibility. Response latency is never substituted for connect time.

HTTP/1.1 requests waiting for a connection-pool slot start their measured time window after a successful initial lease. Start time, elapsed time and latency exclude that pool wait; connection establishment still counts. Availability-timeout and cancelled lease failures retain their original start and wait duration. The surrounding transaction still measures its full wall-clock duration.

HTTP Request Defaults > Protocol & Connections includes Reuse HTTP/2 connections across eligible hosts. It is enabled for new defaults. Existing scripts without the property also enable coalescing. Explicitly disabling the checkbox keeps separate connections per origin. The setting applies to HTTP/2 and the HTTP/2 part of Automatic protocol selection.

Within a virtual user, another host may reuse an established HTTP/2 connection when its DNS addresses include the connected peer address, its port matches, and the certificate covers both hostnames. TLS/client-certificate identities must match. Proxy routes, explicitly bound source addresses, and domain credentials for connection-bound authentication retain separate connections. Requests retain their own authority, cookies, and authentication. Different virtual users never share these connections.

A coalesced response with status 421 disables coalescing for that destination in the current client. Repeatable requests retry once on a dedicated connection; non-repeatable bodies are not replayed. Coalesced requests have an empty connect time because no connection was established for that request. This implements DNS-based coalescing; HTTP/2 ORIGIN-frame discovery is not implemented.

In HTTP Request Defaults, open Protocol & Connections > HTTP/1.1 connections. Maximum connections per host limits the connections available to each virtual user for an origin (scheme, hostname and port). Sequential requests, parallel controllers and embedded-resource downloads share the user's pool. Excess requests wait for a free connection; the parallel controller's concurrency setting does not increase this limit. Configure the limit consistently in the profile's HTTP Request Defaults. Selecting HTTP/1.1 in a new defaults configuration fills in 6. A blank or unset limit also uses 6, including for existing scripts. Explicit positive limits override this default.

Connection availability timeout is the time in milliseconds to wait for a free pooled connection. A positive value bounds the wait, 0 waits indefinitely, and blank keeps the HTTP client's default. A timed-out request reports Connection availability timeout without making a new connection. Successful initial pool waits are excluded from the request time window; failed leases retain their wait. Both fields accept variables and functions. These controls apply to the HTTP/1.1 transport, not HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 streams.

HTTP/1.1 TLS contexts and session caches are shared by sequential and parallel workers of the same virtual user. New connections can resume an earlier TLS session when the server and available tickets allow it; existing open connections need no new handshake. A cold parallel wave is not guaranteed to resume sessions. Contexts are released at user cleanup and replaced on SSL-state reset. Different virtual users remain isolated, including when https.sessioncontext.shared=true; that legacy option now applies only outside virtual users.

HTTP/2 also shares TLS session contexts between a virtual user's clients with the same resolved certificate identity. This includes forced HTTP/2 and negotiating clients. User changes discard both connections and their bound TLS contexts, so new users cannot resume previous users' sessions.

HTTP/3 also shares TLS session contexts between a virtual user's clients, including parallel requests with different timeout or redirect settings. Certificate identities and certificate-retry origins keep separate contexts. New QUIC connections can resume sessions when the server provides usable tickets. User cleanup discards both clients and TLS sessions without affecting other users.

Add Sampler > Dummy Sampler to produce configurable results without network activity. The result type defaults to HTTP. Standard results and statistical aggregate results are also supported. HTTP shows method, HTTP request body, cookies and redirect location; statistical results show sample and error counts. Switching types preserves the hidden values but does not apply them at runtime. Put URL query parameters directly in the URL, for example https://localhost/test?test=bla. The HTTP request body field supplies body content; it does not append parameters to the URL. For HTTP results, the common Request data field supplies additional sampler details after JMeter's generated HTTP request representation. No third-party dummy sampler or monitoring plugin is required.

Common fields cover success, response code/message, request and response data/headers, URL, timestamp, response time, latency, connect/idle time, content type, character encoding, data type, byte sizes, and local/destination endpoints, protocol and TLS versions. The sampler name is the result label. Leave the timestamp blank to anchor the sample interval at invocation time, including when simulating a response delay. An explicit epoch-millisecond timestamp follows the native start/end timestamp setting. Statistical timestamps report the end time. Thread identity/counts, source location, transactions and assertion results are supplied by the test engine. Received bytes follow the native result model: header bytes plus body bytes. A body size of zero uses the actual response bytes. Binary response bytes can be supplied as Base64 with decoding enabled; set the data type to bin to identify binary content.

Fields accept JMeter variables and functions, including timing expressions such as ${__Random(50,500)}. Numeric values must be non-negative integers; sample count must be positive and error count cannot exceed it. Boolean fields accept true or false. Invalid values produce a failed DUMMY_ERROR result with a diagnostic message. Enable Simulate response time to sleep for the configured response time; otherwise results are generated immediately with the configured elapsed time. Simulated waits can be interrupted when stopping the test. Timings and success are independently configurable to support synthetic edge cases.
BreakTest includes additional native utility functions for hashing, encoding, string manipulation, conditional values, environment variables and epoch timestamps.

Proxy settings apply in order: global properties, HTTP Request Defaults, then the HTTP request sampler. An empty proxy section leaves the broader settings in effect. Setting any proxy field makes that scope's routing policy authoritative: with no filter, the proxy is used for all hosts. A host filter replaces broader filters, including global http.nonProxyHosts rules. Unspecified endpoint fields (host, port, and scheme) are filled from broader settings, so a filter-only override can use the proxy host from system.properties or command-line options. Global proxy credentials are used only when the proxy host comes from global settings; a locally configured proxy host does not receive global credentials.

Choose Only matching hosts to proxy only included destinations, or Exclude matching hosts to connect directly for excluded destinations. None is the default host filter. The separate Bypass proxy (connect directly) checkbox forces direct connections and disables the proxy endpoint and filter controls. A sampler-level bypass overrides a filter on HTTP Request Defaults. A section with no endpoint fields, no filter, and bypass unchecked does not save a local override.

Separate hostnames or IP literals with newlines, commas, or semicolons. Exact hosts match case-insensitively; *.example.com matches subdomains (including nested subdomains), but not example.com itself. Include both patterns to cover both. Trailing dots and internationalized hostnames are normalized; bracketed and expanded IPv6 literals are supported. Matching performs no DNS lookups. Ports, URL paths, CIDR ranges, general globs, and regular expressions are not supported. Inclusion and exclusion modes require at least one pattern. Invalid patterns or incomplete endpoints with an explicit proxy policy fail the sample before it sends a request. Older plans without an explicit policy retain direct connections when the proxy endpoint is incomplete. Request hostnames are matched leniently; strict hostname validation applies only to configured patterns. Expressions are resolved at runtime, and parsed policies are reused until the resolved configuration changes.

Filtered-out destinations connect directly, without falling back to another proxy. A proxy connection or authentication failure never triggers direct fallback. Filters apply to HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, SSE connections, redirect destinations (including automatic redirects), and embedded resources. HTTP/3 can use a destination that the policy routes directly; destinations requiring a proxy still fail because the HTTP/3 transport does not support proxies. WebSocket Connect inherits the proxy fields, host filters, and bypass setting from HTTP Request Defaults, falling back to the shared HTTP proxy settings (http.proxyHost, http.proxyPort, and http.nonProxyHosts) for both ws and wss. This replaces the JDK default proxy selector: plans previously relying on https.proxyHost or SOCKS properties must configure an HTTP proxy through these shared settings or HTTP Request Defaults instead. Other HTTP Request Defaults fields are not applied to WebSocket samplers. Both ws:// and wss:// connections use HTTP CONNECT tunnels through an HTTP proxy. HTTPS proxy endpoints are not supported by the JDK WebSocket transport. Proxy authentication follows the JDK HTTP client's authentication policy (including jdk.http.auth.tunneling.disabledSchemes). Credentials are scoped to the selected proxy. Routing is resolved once when opening the connection; reconnect an existing session to apply changed settings. Enable debug logging for org.apache.jmeter.protocol.http.sampler.HTTPHCAbstractImpl to inspect routing decisions. Proxy credentials are omitted from these diagnostics.

Add Client Certificate Config from Add > Config Element inside a shared profile, a named profile, or a thread group. It applies to HTTPS requests (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3) and secure WebSocket connection handshakes. A thread group's explicit certificate config overrides the selected profile; the selected profile overrides the shared profile. A closer config under a controller or request overrides its ancestors. The whole configuration is selected together: fields from different certificate configs are not combined.

Choose Inherit, Use certificate, or Send no client certificate. Inherit uses the outer scope, ultimately falling back to the existing global SSL Manager settings. Use certificate accepts a keystore path, type (PKCS12, JKS or JCEKS; PKCS12 by default), password and alias. Relative paths resolve against the test plan directory. The store must contain a private key and its certificate chain; certificate-only files and separate PEM certificate/key files must first be packaged into a keystore. The same password is used to unlock the store and its private-key entries. Hardware tokens and operating-system certificate stores are not supported by this file-based configuration. A blank path uses the global keystore and its type; a blank password in that case uses the global password. An alias may be omitted only if the store contains exactly one private-key entry. Missing files, incorrect passwords, unknown aliases and unresolved variables fail the request rather than falling back to another identity.

For example, put an employee keystore in the selected profile, and override it with a partner keystore in one thread group. To select a certificate per virtual user, set the alias to ${clientCertAlias} and supply that variable from a CSV Data Set Config or initialization script. The keystore path and password also accept variables. Assign the values once per user when its identity should remain stable; CSV data normally advances every iteration. Use password variables supplied at runtime: a literal password is stored in the JMX file even though the editor masks it. Each distributed worker needs access to its own keystore files and password values; the configuration does not transfer certificates.

Connections and TLS contexts are isolated by resolved certificate identity. A changed alias selects a separate HTTP client instead of reusing a connection authenticated with the previous certificate. WebSocket connections keep their identity until they are closed or reconnected. The legacy Keystore Configuration element retains its global behavior; use Client Certificate Config for scoped overrides. Without a scoped configuration, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 select a global keystore alias when creating a cached client and reuse that identity for its lifetime. Global alias rotation does not create a new client on each request.

HTTP Request Defaults includes a Headers tab with the same add, edit, and remove controls as HTTP Request. Use it for shared headers such as Accept or headers whose values use JMeter variables. Headers are saved with the Defaults element in the test plan.

Request-specific headers take priority. For inherited headers, HTTP Request Defaults and HTTP Header Managers follow scope order: the configuration closest to the request wins, matching header names case-insensitively. At the same scope, the first configuration in tree order wins. For example, a plan-level Defaults value of Accept: */* is overridden by a Thread Group Header Manager with Accept: application/json. Headers with different names are combined; repeated headers within one configuration are preserved unless a closer configuration overrides that name.

ul.li: The built-in HTTP sampler path uses Apache HttpClient 5.
HTTP/2 and HTTP/2-preferred protocol selection are available through the async HttpClient 5 path.
BreakTest handles negotiated fallback, HTTP/2 upload content length, connect-time reporting, and safer replay behavior.
HTTP/2 resource usage was reduced by limiting reactor threads and avoiding unnecessary client/reactor rebuilds between same-user iterations.
NTLM authentication was fixed on the HttpClient 5 path, including variable resolution before async authentication callbacks.
Brotli and Zstandard response decoding were added alongside gzip and deflate.

section.p: Choose Specific request to build a new flow or make a focused change. It is selected by default when the selected Thread Group has no samplers, including an empty Test Plan. The agent interprets the requested outcome from your instructions and the current plan; no separate generation mode or keyword-based routing is needed. Focused edits do not trigger the generation replay or a full recording-repair workflow. AI Repair discovers installed samplers, controllers, timers and processors from the same catalog as the Add menu, then reads native defaults, property types, choices and supported table schemas before creating elements. It can configure HTTP arguments and request bodies, Header Managers and WebSocket handshake headers, including Sec-WebSocket-Protocol. New elements participate in backup, undo and the AI change list.

For example, request a charger simulation and specify the OCPP version, endpoint, authentication and desired messages. The agent can assemble Connect, Send/Wait, Match handlers, paced loops and background Fork branches using native elements. Missing configuration remains a labelled placeholder. For newly generated flows, Specific request requests one bounded synthetic integration replay by default, using a loopback fixture and native timers, unless the user explicitly opts out. Requested assertions are added before replay. Temporary endpoint overrides are restored and fixtures stopped afterward. Offline checks alone are not an integration pass; missing coverage or an infeasible fixture must be reported explicitly. Synthetic validation does not establish compatibility with a real server.

Native creation/configuration tools return compact confirmations by default, avoiding repeated payload and script echoes. Use compact=false when full element details are needed. Catalog discovery is paginated, and the agent is instructed to reuse schemas and batch independent operations. Unsaved plans without an explicitly configured AI working directory use a separate temporary task directory, shown in the activity log; saved plans retain their directory. Generated fixtures remain there for inspection. Codex usage summaries distinguish cached and uncached input when reported; input totals accumulate across model requests and already include cached input. Successful template reports still show unverified behavior and limitations under Follow-up.

Add an SSE Connect sampler. It provides the same URL, parameters, headers, body, files, and advanced settings as HTTP Request, with an SSE tab for session settings and a Recorded Events tab. The request returns after HTTP 200 event-stream headers arrive; events continue arriving in the background. The regular HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 transport retains HTTP headers, cookies, authentication, proxy and TLS settings. HTTP/3 is not supported for SSE. Set a unique session name for each concurrent stream. SSE Connect reuses compatible existing HTTP connections: an idle connection for HTTP/1.1, or a shared connection with concurrent streams for HTTP/2. An occupied HTTP/1.1 connection requires another connection. In the SSE tab, When session already exists controls repeated execution, including later iterations: Close and reconnect (default) replaces only that named stream; Reuse if connected keeps the live stream's original URL, settings and SSE Match actions, or reconnects if it ended; Fail if exists fails when the name is still registered, without disturbing its stream. Use SSE Close to remove it.

Add an SSE Match child through SSE Connect's Add menu and place actions beneath it. Match the event data using exact text or a regular expression, optionally restricted to an event name. The matching data can be saved in a variable; the previous result contains the data, with the event name in the response message and event name/ID in the response headers. Child actions run asynchronously in the virtual user's context, with their normal assertions, extractors and listeners. Each handler has a bounded queue of 64 messages or 4 MiB, allowing one larger event within the configured event limit; overflow reports a failed sample and stops that handler. Each handler receives its own event result. Count incoming messages as samples in the SSE tab defaults to enabled. Disable it to exclude incoming events from sample counts and results. SSE Match actions still execute and report their own samples; stream failures remain visible. Incoming sample naming offers Prefix + event name (for example, prefix Notifications / produces Notifications / ready) or Fixed name to group every event under one sample name. A blank prefix preserves request name / event name; a blank fixed name uses the request name. Unnamed events use message. The inline example updates while editing. Naming only changes reported incoming samples; SSE Match still receives the original event name and data.

The parser handles UTF-8, multiline data, named events, persistent IDs, comments and CR/LF line endings. Maximum event size is configurable in characters (default 1,048,576 characters); incomplete events at EOF are discarded. New SSE requests include Accept: text/event-stream in their editable Headers list. The server must respond with Content-Type: text/event-stream and SSE-formatted data. Response timeout defaults to 0 (no read timeout) for new and imported SSE requests, so quiet streams remain open. Configure a finite read timeout in Advanced when inactivity should fail the request. Existing requests retain their configured timeout. The sampler makes one connection attempt: it does not automatically reconnect or act on retry fields. Use another SSE Connect execution to reconnect. Streams close automatically when the virtual user ends; use SSE Close with the session name to stop receiving earlier. It cancels only that request/stream; HTTP/2 connections remain available for other requests and streams. Receiving stops immediately; the HTTP/2 transport sends the stream reset when the peer next sends data. Closing an already closed session is harmless.

A new-user iteration closes the previous user's SSE sessions before resetting variables, regardless of the existing-session choice. Select Same user on each iteration and Reuse if connected to keep a stream across iterations. An explicit HTTP/2 connection reset also ends streams using that connection.

HAR import recognizes EventSource, text/event-stream, _breaktest.sse and _serverSentEvents. It creates an SSE Connect sampler. The recording archive retains event timestamps, names, IDs, multiline data, transaction IDs/names and capture metadata. The Recorded Events tab shows the captured events, with payload previews limited to 64 Ki characters. The archive retains the full data. Incoming recordings are reference data; add match handlers for the live behavior needed by the test. A recording ending does not imply a client close, so import does not invent an SSE Close step.

AI Repair exposes WebSocket session and Send/Wait settings, searches recorded text, hex and ASCII, and retrieves paged message evidence with direction, relative timestamps and lossless byte previews. It suggests exact earlier-received token matches as correlation candidates for review, including embedded ASCII tokens in binary messages. These candidates are not proof of a dynamic field. The live update_websocket_open_plan tool edits existing Connect, Send, Close and Match settings with undo/change tracking; add_websocket_match_open_plan creates a handler for unsolicited messages. Binary validation responses are labelled hex and include byte length and truncation. Text extractors belong on a Send and Wait response or a captured Match message, not the Connect handshake. Binary application protocols require a proven decoder/encoder and byte-aware extraction/assertions; AI Repair does not automatically infer arbitrary MessagePack, protobuf, compressed or encrypted schemas.

WebSocket Send has an Action setting: Send only or Send and Wait. Send only disables and ignores all waiting options. Send and Wait enables the timeout and response-selection settings; only the matching fields relevant to the selected wait mode are enabled.

The HAR importer recognizes WebSocket connections and creates WebSocket Connect samplers. Imported connections are named websocket-1, websocket-2, and so on in chronological order, counting only selected WebSocket connections. When recording data is retained, their Recorded messages tab lists captured messages in recording order, with milliseconds relative to the connection's startedDateTime, sent/received direction, and message type. Times display three decimal places. Message payloads are stored as base64 in the recording archive. The viewer automatically displays text frames as UTF-8 and binary frames as hexadecimal bytes; select Text or Binary hex to override the display for inspection. The importer also inserts outgoing text and binary messages as WebSocket Send samplers in chronological order, including sends in later transactions. They use Send only and the recorded offset from connection start. A send waits only for the remaining time until that offset; if preceding work runs late, it sends immediately. Observed client-initiated disconnects produce a WebSocket Close sampler at the recorded close initiation time (or the observed close time when initiation time is unavailable), including in later transactions. Server-initiated or unattributed disconnects and stopping a recording do not create a client Close step. Close samplers close immediately when executed; recorded timestamps only determine their position in the script. Handshake response headers and close attribution remain available in the recording archive. Received messages remain reference data. Protocol control frames are handled by the WebSocket transport.

Add WebSocket Connect, WebSocket Send, and WebSocket Close from the Samplers menu. Connect takes a ws:// or wss:// URL and a required session name. Send and Close select that name. Each virtual user owns its sessions, so multiple connections can coexist in one user and different users can use the same name. Close a session before reusing its name. Sessions persist across iterations and are aborted when the user thread ends.

ul.li: Connect owns the session policy, fixed for the lifetime of that connection. View Results Tree displays its HTTP upgrade as a GET request, with the HTTP/HTTPS URL, query parameters, request headers, and response headers. Successful upgrades show 101 Switching Protocols; rejected handshakes retain their HTTP status and response data. Reusing an existing connection does not report another handshake.

Count incoming messages as samples defaults to enabled. Each complete incoming text or binary message produces a separate successful sample through the listeners in scope of Connect, including JTL and aggregate listeners. Disable this to discard incoming messages. No Receive sampler is needed.

Fail on unexpected disconnect defaults to enabled. A server-initiated close (including status 1000) or transport error produces one failed disconnect sample, even when incoming messages are ignored. WebSocket Close and thread-end cleanup do not produce unexpected-disconnect failures. Close waits for the peer's close handshake; a timeout still fails the Close sampler.
Ignore text matching regex discards complete messages for which the Java regular expression finds a match. Empty means no text filter. Use anchors for full-message matching.
Ignore binary prefix discards messages beginning with the supplied hexadecimal bytes, for example 0102. Empty means no binary filter.
Handle ping/pong automatically without samples defaults to enabled. Disable it to count those control frames too. Pong replies are automatic regardless of this setting.
Maximum incoming message bytes defaults to 1048576. An oversized message aborts the session. Fragmented messages are assembled before filtering and counting.

Send transmits UTF-8 text, or hexadecimal bytes when Content type is set to Binary (hex). Hex input accepts spaces, tabs and line breaks, including pasted hex rows. Its elapsed time measures sending, not request/response latency.
Connect, Send and Close have positive millisecond timeouts (default 10000). Failed handshakes and timed-out sends or closes release their connections.

Send and Wait subscribes before sending so immediate replies are captured. Choose Next message for the next complete text or binary message, or Message matching regular expression for a text response matching a Java regex. Matching uses find; use ^hallo$ to match exactly hallo. Choose Binary message containing hex sequence and set Response binary sequence (hex) to match bytes anywhere within a complete binary response, for example 07 95 03 80 A1 30 03 C0. Spaces, tabs and line breaks are ignored; the sequence must contain at least one complete byte. Matching spans fragments of one message, but never separate messages. Connect filters apply before matching; ping/pong never satisfies a wait. Unrelated messages follow Connect's incoming-sample policy without completing the wait. The matching response becomes the sampler response, without an extra incoming sample, and supports normal assertions, extractors and thread error handling.

Wait timeout (milliseconds) is separate from the send timeout and defaults to 10000. It limits waiting after sending completes; unrelated messages never restart it. Expiry fails the sampler and leaves the session available for subsequent operations. Only one wait may be active per session. Previously received messages are not queued for a later wait.

section.p: Incoming samples run on the transport callback thread. They record the originating user thread name and the sample_variables values captured at Connect. They do not execute assertions, extractors, timers, transaction-controller aggregation, or thread stop-on-error actions. Put listeners at the thread group or above when all sessions should report to them. Asynchronous listener notifications are serialized per virtual user, run outside session locks and have access to the originating user's variables. Ordinary per-thread listeners are cloned for this callback path; globally shared listeners must still support concurrent calls. Script listeners can update user variables, but their timing relative to the main flow remains asynchronous.

The transport uses Java's built-in WebSocket client and adds no dependencies. BreakTest's pinned HttpClient 5.6.1 does not provide the optional WebSocket module introduced in HttpClient 5.7. WebSocket Connect reuses the HTTP Cookie Manager in its test-plan scope. Cookies received by previous HTTP requests are selected at each handshake using the same domain, path, expiry and Secure rules as HTTP: ws is treated as http, and wss as https. Variable-backed cookie values are resolved on the virtual user's thread. Cookies are sent during the opening handshake; they are not attached to individual WebSocket messages. Set-Cookie response headers from successful upgrades and rejected handshakes are imported into the same user's Cookie Manager on the user thread, using the normal cookie validation rules. Concurrent successful upgrades are correlated by their unique WebSocket handshake keys, including when users connect to the same URL through a shared transport client. Cookies are available to subsequent HTTP requests and WebSocket connects. Each handshake request is attributed to the user that started it, so users sharing a transport client connect concurrently and never wait for another user's handshake. Rejected, timed-out and cancelled handshakes leave shared clients available; late responses cannot populate another user's store. With Same user on each iteration disabled, open WebSockets are closed before user variables reset, even if an error skipped the Close sampler. Same-user iterations retain their named sessions until a sampler closes or replaces them. Connect's When session already exists setting applies on every execution, including subsequent same-user iterations. Close and reconnect (the default) disposes the previous connection for that name and performs a fresh handshake. Reuse if connected keeps an open connection with its original URL, headers, and session settings; a disconnected session is replaced. Reuse reports success without a handshake. Fail if exists reports an error without changing the existing session. Other named sessions are unaffected. An explicit Close sampler fails if the connection is already closed or the session is missing, even when unexpected-disconnect reporting is disabled. Closing an already disconnected session still removes its registry entry. In new-user mode, the old sessions have already been cleared, so all three options create a fresh connection.

WebSocket Match controllers under Connect react to application messages in the background while the main script continues. Adding Connect in the GUI creates an empty Match child; use Connect's Add menu to add more. Each Match has an exact text, text regular expression (find), or binary hex sequence condition. Hex accepts spaces and newlines and matches anywhere in a binary frame. Every matching block runs, in arrival order within that block; different Match blocks run concurrently. Normal samplers and controllers can be nested underneath, including HTTP Request, WebSocket Send, Transaction Controller, assertions, and extractors. Native control ping/pong frames do not trigger these handlers. Incoming-message sample filters and Send and Wait consumption do not suppress application handlers.

The editor has three rows: match type, matching value, and optional Save message to variable. Leave the variable name empty to store nothing. Otherwise the complete matching text message is saved unchanged, or the complete binary payload is saved as a lossless hex string. The variable is updated before that handler block runs and remains available to later steps in the same virtual user's script. No automatic prefix or regex-capture variables are created. For example, match exact text ping and place a WebSocket Send with payload pong below it. For page-ready messages, match regex process ready for page: (.*?) done and save to receivedMessage. A script or extractor can then read ${receivedMessage} and extract the page number before an HTTP request. Configure nested WebSocket samplers with the same session name as Connect. Each virtual user has its own variables and cookies; handlers of the same user share them. Use distinct save-variable names for concurrent Match blocks if their messages must remain separate.

Each Match parks its background worker while idle. Its pending queue is bounded to 64 messages and 4 MiB; overflow stops that handler and reports WS_HANDLER_OVERFLOW. Close, disconnect and replacement stop handlers after any block already running completes, so a handler can close its own session; queued messages are discarded. New-user iteration and thread shutdown stop handlers immediately. Same-user iterations retain them when the connection is retained, including when a Fork Controller error ends the iteration; Connect's reuse mode retains the original handlers and settings. Handlers have their own transaction scope and their samples use the normal engine processing path. Assertions, timers, pre- and post-processors attached to Connect apply to Connect only; its config elements and listeners also apply to handler samples. The main script must remain running for background handlers to run.

The HTTP Headers tab on Connect uses the same header editor as HTTP Request. HTTP Header Managers in scope also apply. Connect's own headers take priority, then the closest scoped manager, with case-insensitive name matching and repeated values preserved within a manager. Names and values can use JMeter variables. When the Cookie Manager supplies matching cookies, they replace any manually configured Cookie header, following the HTTP sampler's behavior. The JDK controls Host, Connection, Upgrade, Content-Length, Expect, and Sec-WebSocket-* handshake headers; attempts to set those in Connect's own header table fail Connect. Transport-owned headers inherited from HTTP Header Managers are ignored. The Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header is imported and negotiated as a comma-separated list of subprotocols. Handshake keys are regenerated for each connection; compression extensions are not imported because the transport does not support them. Request views preserve the original ws:// or wss:// URL. Secure WebSockets reuse the HTTP SSL Manager's certificate stores and permissive server-certificate policy, including self-signed certificates and hostname mismatches. Client certificate aliases are resolved on the user thread at Connect, including aliases from variables. Reconnecting reevaluates the alias. Transport clients are shared only within the same SSL Manager, certificate stores and selected client alias, preventing TLS session reuse across identities. User sessions, headers and cookies remain isolated. Transport tasks use virtual threads; the last session releases its shared client. Unlike HTTP/1.1's per-user SSL contexts, WebSocket clients share TLS session caches across users with the same identity. This can reduce full TLS handshake load and is independent of https.sessioncontext.shared. For mutual TLS, use a certificate-alias variable to select the same identity explicitly in HTTP and WebSocket samplers; automatic round-robin selection advances per connection. HTTP TLS protocol and cipher settings also apply to WebSocket clients. Proxy settings and filters come from HTTP Request Defaults or the shared HTTP proxy properties, as described above. Authorization Manager is not inherited; an explicit Authorization header is supported. WebSocket replay supports HTTP/1.1 WebSocket Upgrade, not HTTP/2 Extended CONNECT or permessage-deflate.

In View Results Tree, choose Binary to inspect response bytes as hexadecimal with byte offsets and a printable ASCII column. The three columns scroll together and can be selected independently, so copying multiple rows of hex or ASCII preserves the 16-byte line breaks without including other columns. Non-printable bytes appear as dots. The view works for WebSocket and HTTP responses, preserves the original bytes, and respects view.results.tree.max_size, marking truncated displays. Hex previews additionally default to 65536 bytes via view.results.tree.binary.max_bytes, avoiding a multi-megabyte hex expansion. Text view decodes binary responses on a best-effort basis.

Message payloads may contain control characters such as SignalR's record separator (0x1E). Values that XML 1.0 cannot represent are saved with a Base64 UTF-16 marker and restored unchanged. These marked properties require this BreakTest version or later; older readers do not decode the marker and must not be used for these plans.

The reference plugin was reviewed at commit c599598e6f4023a88815fdf140338cb9c19f5e00. Its README identifies LGPL, its distribution includes GPLv3 and LGPLv3 license texts, and its source headers specify LGPL version 3 or later. The GPL text is incorporated by the LGPL; its presence does not mean the plugin is simply GPL-only.

We can study its documented behavior and independently implement session handling, filters, fragmentation, and close semantics. Copying or adapting its implementation would require preserving the applicable LGPL terms, notices and source obligations; copied code cannot simply be relabeled Apache-2.0. Linking it as a separate replaceable library is another option, with LGPL distribution, source and relinking obligations. Obtaining a separate compatible license from the relevant rights holders would be another route to direct reuse. This implementation copies no plugin source and does not depend on its binary. It reuses BreakTest's sampler, TestBean GUI, listener and result infrastructure and the JDK's RFC 6455 implementation.

ul.li: Lazy response decompression stores compressed bytes and decompresses only when response data is accessed.
Response retention modes can keep compressed data, discard successful bodies, keep only failing bodies, or retain MD5 checksums.
Lightweight test-plan cloning reduces per-thread object churn.
Header merging, temporary property handling, response read buffers, and diagnostic metadata paths were optimized.
Rich sample diagnostics are lazy and listener-driven, so normal load runs avoid unnecessary per-sample storage.

section.p: BreakTest moves load modeling into a unified Thread Group rather than splitting common scenarios across several specialized thread groups.

ul.li: Closed-model schedules can combine different ramp-up speeds, hold periods, and target thread counts.
Open-model schedules can model arrivals, use even-arrival helpers, and cap active threads.
Thread Group pacing controls are available for transaction pacing.
Schedule parsing is safer and includes graph preview support.
Runtime user variables are cleared on new iterations when same-user mode is disabled, while initial variables are preserved.
Pause and Resume are available in the GUI and through bin/pause.* and bin/resume.*.
In closed model, pause holds active threads and stops further ramp-up.
In open model, pause stops new arrivals and lets active threads finish naturally, so load drops while paused.
Shutdown no longer waits for timers to complete; it waits for in-flight server responses to finish cleanly.

section.p: Add a Weighted Switch Controller from the Logic Controllers menu to randomly run one direct child each time the controller is entered. The table automatically lists child samplers and controllers, including transactions and modules. Configuration elements are not selectable branches.

Edit the Weight column to set a finite, non-negative number. New children default to 1. Weights are relative: 3 and 1 give probabilities of 75% and 25%; they do not need to add up to 100. Decimals are supported. Zero-weight and disabled children are excluded. If no child has a positive weight, the controller runs nothing. Invalid weights are rejected in the editor and fail execution if introduced directly into a plan file.

A chosen controller runs its entire branch. Selection happens once per iteration, independently for each virtual user; observed proportions converge over many iterations rather than enforcing exact quotas. An empty or completed selected branch does not fall through to another child.

Weights are saved on the child elements, so they survive renaming, reordering, copying and saving/reopening the plan, including children with duplicate names. Moving a weighted child into another Weighted Switch Controller retains its weight. The Enabled column is read-only; enable or disable children in the test tree.

ul.li: Parallel Controller runs child samplers concurrently with bounded scheduling.
Fork Controller starts asynchronous child branches that share virtual-user context and complete before thread teardown.
HTTP state handling was tightened to reduce unsafe sharing in concurrent paths.

section.p: Graceful shutdown lets in-flight parallel requests finish. Immediate cancellation waits up to jmeterthread.parallel.shutdown_timeout milliseconds for all branches of a parallel controller together (default 1000; 0 skips the wait). Keep this setting below jmeterengine.threadstop.wait so the owner can finish within the engine's stop deadline.

If a branch ignores interruption beyond this deadline, BreakTest logs a warning naming the remaining branches and stops its virtual user. The user cannot start another iteration, and late sample results are omitted, even if they report success. Thread-finished callbacks and user resource cleanup are deferred until all lingering parallel branches and associated forks exit. Deferred callbacks run on a separate daemon thread with the owner's JMeter context; plugins should not rely on the original Java thread's thread-local state for this exceptional cleanup path.

Java cannot safely force an uncooperative sampler to exit. Its resources remain retained until it returns; daemon parallel workers and deferred cleanup do not keep the JVM alive. Normal shutdown retains synchronous cleanup after workers finish.

BreakTest includes local agent and MCP support for AI-assisted script repair. Tools such as Codex, Claude Code, Cursor Agent, Gemini CLI, Pi Code, OpenCode, and Copilot CLI can inspect a JMX script, validate it, repair it, and show changes in the GUI.

ul.li: Create or repair extractors and correlations.
Parameterize dynamic values.
Add assertions.
Fix selectors and unstable recorded data.
Review generated changes from the GUI before continuing.
Cleaner light/dark GUI styling.
Undo and redo for semantic tree edits including add, delete, update, move, and search/replace operations.
Background JMX loading with a loading overlay.
Fast GUI loading is enabled by default. Set breaktest.gui.load.fast=false for compatibility with components that require editor initialization on load.
Missing plugin elements load as disabled placeholders instead of failing the whole file.
Search Tree can flag pre-processors, post-processors, assertions, timers, and config elements.

Search scope offers a dropdown for one Thread Group or All, with checkboxes for names, paths, headers, parameters, raw bodies, recorded requests, recorded responses, and other fields. All field areas are selected by default; Select all and Select none simplify changing them. Header and parameter columns can be restricted to names or values. Search and Replace respects the selected areas and columns; recorded traffic remains read-only. Scope choices and dialog sizes are remembered while working on the same plan.

The removal target can be whole elements, header rows, parameter rows, or both row types. Row previews show the owning element, row number, and matching data. Row removal respects the selected Thread Group and Search in areas and preserves samplers, Header Managers, and HTTP Request Defaults. Raw bodies and recorded traffic cannot be deleted as parameter or header rows.

Show Matches for Removal opens a resizable review dialog; select the results to remove, then choose Remove Selected. After removal, an optional cleanup prompt lists controllers emptied by that removal, including empty parents. Previously empty controllers and Thread Groups are preserved. Both previews offer Select all/none, show the selected count, and disable removal when nothing is selected. Completion reports skipped rows that changed, disappeared, or became busy. Each replacement or removal (including controller cleanup) is a single undoable action; undo and redo refresh the open editor.

section.p: The recorder forwards traffic independently of the sampler selected for replay. HTTPS recording negotiates the same protocol on both TLS connections: HTTP/2 when supported by the browser and origin, or HTTP/1.1 otherwise. HTTP/2 frames, including flow control and multiplexed streams, pass through unchanged. HTTP/3 is not supported. Compressed bodies, duplicate headers, multipart boundaries, chunk extensions and trailers are preserved. Responses stream to the browser as they arrive, and persistent connections can carry multiple requests. WebSocket upgrades are relayed bidirectionally and recorded as native WebSocket connections and messages.

Native recordings in the JMX archive retain the original client-facing HTTP messages (before TLS encryption), including encoded bodies and transfer framing. HTTP/2 recordings retain original per-stream frames alongside decoded headers; HPACK frames refer to the shared connection compression context. The recorded-data views still show decoded content for inspection. A streaming exchange is finalized when it ends or the recorder stops. Transport failures retain available partial data and appear in the finish-recording wizard with diagnostic details. Failed requests are not automatically resent. Sampler conversion, archive storage, and HTTP/2 header inspection run on recording workers, independently of forwarding.

Request headers are always included in generated samplers. Store recorded requests/responses (enabled by default) controls whether original request/response headers and bodies are retained as native recorded exchanges for later inspection. Disabling storage still creates samplers with request headers, grouping, and timing; it does not change forwarded traffic. The former Capture HTTP Headers setting is ignored when loading existing scripts or preferences.

Responses with Content-Type: text/event-stream become native SSE Connect samplers, as in HAR import. The proxy records complete events with their names, IDs, multiline data, arrival times, and active recorder transaction names. HTTP, HTTPS, HTTP/2, chunked transfer, and supported content encodings retain their original forwarded bytes; SSE parsing and decompression run on a separate recording worker. With recording storage enabled, events and original HTTP bytes survive saving and reopening the JMX archive. Stopping the recorder or closing an SSE stream from the browser preserves complete events and discards an unfinished event, without marking the capture as failed. Browser HTTP/2 CANCEL/NO_ERROR resets are treated as normal SSE cancellation; server resets and protocol errors remain failures. Stream duration does not extend a transaction or force unrelated requests into one parallel group. Incoming events remain reference data; the recorder does not invent SSE Match actions or a Close step.

WebSocket connections are recorded as native WebSocket Connect, Send, and Close samplers, using the same conversion as HAR import. Both plain and TLS connections are supported, including WebSocket streams carried by HTTP/2 extended CONNECT. Session names use websocket-1, websocket-2, or sse-1, sse-2, skipping names already present in the test plan. Outgoing text and binary messages become timed Send samplers; incoming messages and control frames remain available as recorded reference data. Fragmented messages are assembled and negotiated permessage-deflate payloads are decoded in the background, while forwarded bytes remain unchanged. With Store recorded requests/responses enabled, the native recording retains handshake headers, message directions, payloads, connection-relative times, and original frame bytes. Turning storage off still creates the replay samplers.

Stopping the recorder opens a wizard: choose hostnames with the same grouped selector used by HAR import, review recording failures (skipped only when there are none), then configure transactions and think times. Failures remain visible even for excluded hosts. Select a row to read its full destination and error details. TLS negotiation failures before an HTTP request arrives are shown with the CONNECT destination and cannot be selected for replay. Failed captures are unchecked by default; selected failures are included as enabled samplers with their diagnostic comments. HTTP 4xx/5xx responses are included normally. Choose Review later to keep the pending recording, then use Review recording... to reopen it before starting another session. After adding the recording, the target thread groups expand automatically. Process correlation rules is enabled by default when the selected recording has stored requests/responses. It scans only newly added HTTP and WebSocket Connect requests using the plan's enabled correlation rules, then opens the existing match review before applying extractors and replacements. This includes SignalR negotiation tokens used in a subsequent native WebSocket URL, including URL-encoded tokens. Each thread group is processed separately; consumers that depend on an extractor in the same parallel group use the existing split confirmation. The choice is saved with recorder preferences. Without stored exchanges the option is unavailable; the wizard explains the storage requirement. Non-GUI recording has no wizard and retains failures as disabled samplers. The recorder and wizard show session counts for captured requests (before filtering), filtered requests, failed captures, incomplete captures, and processing errors. Incomplete and failed counts can overlap. HTTP/2 inspection failures leave a persistent warning even when no sampler could be created; forwarding continues, and observed streams without captures are counted when the connection ends. Diagnostics identify browser/server I/O failures and recorder shutdown where known. Warnings remain after review until the next recording starts.

Requests are ordered by their recorded start time, with a capture sequence breaking ties. The recorder reuses HAR import's transaction layout and delay modes. Recorder parallel groups retain connected overlaps, including requests that start while an earlier slow request is still running. Redirect targets start a new group. A shared monotonic clock retains sub-millisecond start/end precision for grouping. Idle gaps are measured after the latest preceding response ends, so a slow overlapping request does not create false think time. The defaults are a new Transaction Controller per group, as-recorded think time, and no automatic or followed redirects; redirect requests are recorded individually. Transactions follow the names set during recording; elapsed idle time does not start a new transaction. Transaction-name edits take effect on Enter or when focus leaves the name field. Sampler names omit query strings by default, without changing the recorded URL or replay parameters. Use #{path}#{querystring} (or #{path}#querystring) in the name formatter to include the query; the query placeholder includes the leading question mark only when a query is present. The recorder defaults to appending _preflight to OPTIONS request names, as HAR import does. Disable Append _preflight to OPTIONS request names to keep those names unchanged; this preference is saved with recorder settings. Incomplete captures and event streams do not extend transaction activity; their native recordings retain the actual transfer timings. Transaction boundaries are resolved before filtering hosts or failed captures. Think-time choices only affect replay delays. The first transaction has no think time. Existing explicit legacy grouping choices remain available. Each request snapshots its target, naming format and prefix, grouping, exchange storage, GraphQL detection, replay redirect, keep-alive, image-download, and ignore-error settings when it arrives. Later edits do not change requests already in flight or waiting for background conversion. The wizard's final layout choices still apply to the reviewed recording.

Remember recorder settings for other scripts saves recorder preferences, including the naming format, filters, grouping, redirects, and think-time settings, to user.properties under proxy.recorder.*. Existing script settings take precedence when that script is opened. Host and failure selections apply only to the current recording.

Use File > Import OpenAPI JSON... to turn an OpenAPI 3.x or Swagger 2.0 JSON file into an editable Test Fragment named after info.title (or the filename when no title is supplied). Each HTTP operation becomes a request named with its method and path. Simple Controllers group requests by the first operation tag, falling back to the first path segment for untagged operations.

The importer includes optional parameters and request-body properties, resolves references within the file, combines allOf schemas, and chooses the first oneOf or anyOf alternative. Explicit examples, defaults, constants and enum values supply sample data; otherwise it generates stable, field-specific placeholders: repeated field names reuse the same generated value when their constraints agree, while different fields get distinctive samples suitable for search/replace. Numeric samples prefer eight digits, subject to format, bounds and multiples; strings include a field-specific token. Explicit examples, defaults and enums remain unchanged. Booleans and narrowly constrained fields may share values. Read-only properties are excluded and recursive schemas stop with a null placeholder. Review generated values for application-specific constraints before running. Query parameters, including GET parameters, remain in the URL path for search/replace and to keep them separate from request bodies. Header and cookie parameters appear in each sampler's native Headers tab. Requests include User-Agent and Accept headers (using response media types when declared), and requests with bodies include the matching Content-Type. Explicit header values are preserved, except that OpenAPI 3 Accept, Content-Type and Authorization header parameters are ignored as the specification requires. JSON, text, URL-encoded and multipart form request bodies are supported. Requests with other body media types, and multipart file fields, are still imported; a warning after the import lists what to add by hand. External references produce an import error without adding a partial fragment.

Hostname, protocol and port are left empty to inherit HTTP Request Defaults. Request paths start with the path of the first effective server URL (using server variable defaults) or the Swagger basePath. Operation servers override path-level servers, which override document-level servers; server hosts are not copied. Configure authentication through your usual shared defaults or header manager. Reference the fragment from a Module Controller, or copy its requests into a thread group. Importing a specification does not send requests to the API.

ul.li: View Results Tree shows richer request, response, endpoint, HTTP/TLS, cookie, variable, and binary/text diagnostics.
Jump-to-source support connects samples back to test elements.
BreakTest JMX metadata preserves origin and source-path details.
When BreakTest HAR metadata is present, recorded request/response tabs are shown in View Results Tree and HTTP sampler editors.
Recorded-vs-replayed diffs help debug HAR migration and HTTP/2 replay.
View Results Tree shows a transaction as soon as it starts and adds its samples below it as they complete. The transaction is updated with its timing and status when it finishes.

HAR query parameters and form parameters use the HTTP form encoder to decide whether to enable URL encoding. This includes characters such as @, /, :, and ,, even though some are allowed unescaped in other URL components. Imported parameter names and values remain readable; encoding is applied when sending the request. Compared with earlier imports, more parameters may have URL Encode enabled.

The HAR wizard and Tools > Correlation Rules use grouped built-in, shared custom, and plan-local correlation rules for the supported response extractors. The Tools dialog presents a group/rule tree on the left and the selected rule's settings on the right, distinguishes fixed built-in rules from editable custom rules, and lets you enable or disable individual rules or whole groups. Use Save state to preserve enabled-rule choices across application updates and Process rules to match recorded responses in the selected Thread Group. Its Info button explains how to create a custom rule from an existing extractor.

Built-in groups cover OAuth and OpenID Connect, SAML, Keycloak, Matrix, Apereo CAS, Amazon Cognito, Jenkins, Socket.IO / Engine.IO, Flask-WTF, Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, ASP.NET, JavaServer Faces, Django, Ruby on Rails, Spring Security, Laravel, CSRF meta tags, CSRF cookies and headers, Salesforce, Salesforce Commerce Cloud, SAP, ServiceNow, SharePoint, Drupal, WordPress, Magento, Liferay, Atlassian, PeopleSoft, Oracle ADF, Oracle NCA, Siebel, SignalR, and generic JSON and REST responses. Rules that read a hidden form field or meta tag accept the attributes in either order.

CAS rules cover login and service tickets. Cognito rules cover challenge sessions and nested authentication tokens; cryptographic challenge responses are not generated. Jenkins rules read the crumb issuer JSON response. Engine.IO rules recognize version 4 open packets for HTTP polling; they do not implement WebSocket frame replay.

CSRF cookie/header rules cover Spring and Laravel's XSRF-TOKEN, Django's csrftoken, and dedicated response headers. When a recorded request header uses the URL-decoded response token, its generated reference uses __urldecode to preserve that transformation during replay. Cookie headers themselves remain managed by the Cookie Manager. Rules are only proposed when an extracted value is reused by a later request; competing values and short incidental matches are rejected.
Body rules are skipped for responses whose content type is an image, font, media, stylesheet, or other binary download, since those never carry correlation values and dominate a typical recording.

Built-in rules are shipped in a versioned application resource and may be updated with BreakTest. Its JSON uses a groups array whose objects contain a group name and nested rules. Custom rules use the same structure in bin/predefined-correlations.custom.json, or another JSON file selected with breaktest.predefined_correlations.file in user.properties; the updater preserves this file.

Right-click a Thread Group and choose Process Correlation Rules to scan its recorded responses with the currently enabled rules and review the proposed replacements. Use Tools > Correlation Rules to change the enabled rules. Processing is unavailable while a test is running.

Custom rules can select multiple values for Replacement scope: Parameters (query and form), Query parameters, Form parameters, Path, Body, or Headers. For example, choose Headers and Parameters together. All overrides the other scopes and is the default when no scopes are set. Match whole value only requires complete parameter/header values, complete path segments, or complete tokens in body text; partial matching remains the default. Body token characters are letters, digits, underscore, hyphen, dot, and percent, so 123 does not replace part of 1234 or 123.4. An optional Replacement field pattern uses a Java regex to select regions within each field: only occurrences of the extracted value inside a matching region are replaced. For example, id: \d+ targets that portion of a body without changing other numbers. Patterns can match the value alone or include a parameter/header name, such as ^username=.+$ or ^Authorization: Bearer .+$. Parameter and header patterns limit replacement to their values. During HAR import, parameter patterns are evaluated against recorded text before decoding, so discovery and application select the same occurrences. Default All behavior preserves replacement in editable values exposed by non-HTTP samplers. With no filters, URL matching also supports opaque query text without an equals sign and values spanning query delimiters when the query remains in URL text (WebSocket and POST-style requests). Requests imported as separate query arguments, such as GET, match argument values only. Header names and explicit name=value query keys remain literal; a URL match overlapping any named query key is rejected. These restrictions apply during discovery, review, HAR import, and application. In JSON, the settings are replacementScope (an array of ALL, PARAMETERS, QUERY_PARAMETERS, POST_PARAMETERS, PATH, BODY, HEADERS; older single-string values are also accepted), replacementWholeValue, and replacementFieldPattern. Missing settings retain All, partial matching, and no pattern restriction. Headers excluded from import, including Cookie, remain excluded.

Response-body extractors operate on sampler results and are not HTTP-specific. Correlation discovery can use recorded responses from any sampler; replacement requires the sampler to expose editable fields through Replaceable. Body scope includes WebSocket messages and UDP Data. Other plugins can participate by exposing fields and their search-area metadata. A recorded response is still required to discover an extraction automatically; binary traffic must first be decoded into the representation the extractor expects.

Field patterns are validated before import or saving. When reading existing shared or plan-local catalogs, a rule with an invalid field regex is retained for repair and displays a diagnostic; it makes no replacements, and saving another rule or moving its group does not remove it. Matching has a bounded work budget and supports cancellation; a pattern exceeding the budget skips that field while processing continues for other fields and rules. The scan results and HAR import review display the affected rule and diagnostic, including when the scan finds no correlations. Warnings raised later are also shown when preparing step-by-step review, completing bulk apply, or completing HAR import. Moving a rule changes only its group in each catalog where it already exists, preserving separate shared and plan-local versions.

Each rule also has a minValueLength setting, shown as Minimum value length in the custom rule editor. It defaults to 6 for new and older rules and can be lowered to 1. The threshold counts captured characters after trimming whitespace. Lowering it permits substring matches in request data, including unrelated numbers; use the replacement filters to target the intended fields.

Each rule has a maxMatches setting that defaults to -1 (unlimited). Set a positive limit to reject responses with more than that many occurrences; existing explicit limits remain in effect. Repeated identical captures are compared with later requests only once. BreakTest accepts a correlation only when one distinct captured value is used by later requests and sets the generated extractor's match number to that value's first occurrence. The match number is not predefined in the catalog.

In Tools > Correlation Rules, use Export custom rules... to share all custom rules currently available to the dialog as a standalone JSON file. Built-in rules are excluded and their IDs cannot be overwritten by imported custom rules. Export asks before replacing an existing file. On another installation, use Import custom rules... to merge the file into the installation catalog and current JMX archive; matching rule IDs are replaced and unrelated rules are retained. Save the test plan to persist its updated archive.
Show custom rules only filters the rule browser without changing which rules are enabled for matching. Importing the same file again updates matching IDs rather than adding duplicate rules.

Right-click a Regex, JSONPath, Boundary, CSS, XPath, XPath2, or JSON JMESPath Extractor and choose Save as Custom Predefined Correlation, then select an existing custom group or enter a new group name (leave empty for Custom). One rule browser opens with a saved-count message and the first new rule selected. Select a rule and choose Edit to adjust its replacement filters and other settings; extractors producing multiple rules do not open a chain of dialogs. BreakTest stores the rule in both the custom installation catalog and correlations/custom-predefined-rules.json inside the JMX archive, making it available locally and shippable with the plan. When the parent sampler has a recorded response, the minimum value length is initialized to the shortest non-empty captured value, capped at 6. Without a recording or usable capture it remains 6; default/fallback values do not lower it. Native settings such as CSS attributes, boundaries, and XPath namespaces are retained for discovery and replay.
If and While Controllers support structured condition rows with all/any matching while preserving legacy expressions.

While Controllers have an optional Max iterations field. Leave it blank for no limit, or enter a non-negative integer (including a variable or function resolving to one). Zero skips the loop. The cap applies alongside either condition mode and counts complete iterations independently of the displayed index starting at zero or one. The count resets each time the controller is entered from its parent. Invalid or negative limits stop the loop and log an error.
Loop and while index behavior options are visible and configurable.
Transaction Controller includes measurement modes plus delay and pacing controls.

Transaction Controller has no Generate parent sample option. Every sample is sent to listeners as soon as it completes and links to the transaction it ran in, and the transaction sample follows when the transaction ends. Transactions only keep running totals, never the samples themselves. Plans saved with the old option load unchanged, and the option is not saved again.

Flat result listeners show top-level transactions and samples outside transactions by default. Enable Children on a listener to include child samples and nested transactions in its display and statistics. This applies to live results and loaded result files with transaction IDs; saved result files still contain all samples allowed by the logging filters. Clear the display before a new run, or reload the file, after changing the option. View Results Tree always keeps children expandable under their transaction.
Boundary, CSS/HTML, Regex, XPath, XPath2, JSONPath, and JMESPath extractors support fail-on-no-match behavior.

JSON Data Set Config loads a UTF-8 JSON object or an array of objects into variables. Add it under Config Elements and select the JSON file. Relative filenames resolve against the test plan directory. For {"name":"Alice","payload":{"id":1}}, ${name} is Alice and ${payload} is {"id":1}. An optional prefix such as data. produces ${data.name}. Strings are unquoted, numbers and booleans use JSON text, nulls become empty strings, and nested objects and arrays remain JSON strings. Nested fields are also exposed as variables, for example ${payload.id}. Arrays use one-based indexes and a count: ${addresses_1.city}, ${addresses_2.city}, and ${addresses_matchNr}. Use Copy JSON into archive to include the file in the saved JMX; Use JSON from archive selects that shared copy and Browse selects an archived file. Read first 10 samples previews all variable assignments without advancing the test. Edit JSON edits the selected local or archived file and validates it before saving; a missing file can be created from the editor. Export JSON saves a local copy. One object is allocated per iteration according to Sharing mode. All threads (the default) share a record position for the same file; Current thread group shares within a group; Current thread gives each thread its own position. A custom identifier shares a position among threads using the same file and identifier, even across groups. Different formats, files, and XML Record XPath selections keep separate positions. Prefixes do not split a shared position. Shared positions and cached data reset between test runs. Missing fields and indexed values become empty strings, and missing array counts become zero, so shorter rows do not retain values from earlier rows. Generated names that collide with existing names (for example a.b and a nested a/b) are rejected rather than silently overwriting values. Recycling defaults to enabled; disabling it sets variables to <EOF> after the last record, or stops the thread when Stop thread on EOF is enabled. Empty arrays, invalid JSON, non-object records, and unreadable files stop the thread with an error.

XML Data Set Config provides the same archive copy, file browsing, sample preview, editing, export, variable prefix, sharing modes, recycling, and end-of-file controls as JSON Data Set Config. Record XPath selects one element per iteration: the default /*/* selects children of the document root, while /* treats the root as a single record. For <users><user id="1"><name>Alice</name><age>30</age></user></users>, the variables are ${@id}=1, ${name}=Alice, and ${age}=30. Simple child elements become text values. Nested, attributed, or repeated child elements remain available as XML fragments, with nested values also exposed directly: ${addresses.item_1.city}, ${addresses.item_2.city}, and ${addresses.item_matchNr}. Nested attributes use names such as ${addresses.item_1.@id}. Sibling names repeated anywhere in the selected records are indexed consistently across all rows, even rows with just one such sibling. Elements named item are always indexed. Non-repeated children use dotted paths. The complete XML variables are retained; repeated fragments are concatenated in document order. Records without child elements expose ${#text}. Namespace prefixes are retained in variable names; use XPath local-name() to select namespaced records. Missing fields become empty strings, missing counts become zero, and previews do not advance shared record positions. The editor preserves the XML encoding and validates before saving. DTDs and external entities are disabled. Invalid XML, a missing file, or an XPath selecting no records or non-element nodes stops the thread with an error.

YAML Data Set Config supports UTF-8 .yaml and .yml files with the same archive, preview, editor, export, prefix, sharing modes, and end-of-file controls as JSON. A mapping supplies one record; a list of mappings supplies successive records. Multiple documents separated by --- are read in order, with lists expanded into records. Each mapping key becomes a variable. Strings remain text, null becomes an empty string, and nested lists and mappings remain JSON strings while also exposing the same dotted paths, one-based indexes, and _matchNr counts as JSON. YAML 1.2 JSON-schema scalar rules apply: true and false are booleans, while yes, no, and dates remain strings. Comments, block strings, and non-recursive anchors and aliases are supported. Duplicate or non-string mapping keys, custom tags, recursive aliases, and non-mapping records are rejected. Documents are limited to 3,145,728 code points; expanded input is limited to 100,000 values and 100 nested levels.
CSV Data Set can read records in random order.
CSV preview shows first sample variable assignments.
UDP Request sends datagrams with optional response waiting, response timeout, local address and port binding, and socket reuse.
UDP Receiver can read a later datagram from a named socket created by UDP Request.
A friendly payload-format selector provides UTF-8 text, hexadecimal, and single-byte text; advanced custom codecs can implement the native UDPTrafficCodec interface.
The implementation uses the Java networking API directly and does not require the JMeter Plugins common I/O or common JMeter libraries.

section.p: See Native UDP Request And Receiver for configuration details.

ul.li: RMI Remote Server style distributed execution is removed. Use BreakTest Enterprise or another controlled orchestration layer for distributed runs.
BreakTest-specific JMX metadata may not round-trip into older Apache JMeter versions.
Plugins that depend on removed internals may require migration.
HttpClient 4 runtime jars remain available for legacy plugin compatibility, but the built-in HTTP Request sampler uses HttpClient 5.

section.name: Ignoring sampler results
section.p: The result inclusion menu beside Comments in the shared sampler header offers three modes. Its button displays the selected mode:

ul.li: Included (default): report results normally.
Ignore on success: report only failed results, including assertion failures.
Ignore always: exclude all results from this sampler.

section.p: Transaction elapsed time still includes the ignored request's wait in both Total run time including timers (the default) and Total run time excluding timers. Use Sum child sampler times to leave ignored sampler durations out of the transaction time. This mode sums included child durations rather than measuring wall-clock time, so parallel requests can produce a sum longer than the transaction's actual duration.

With Ignore always, a failed request does not mark its enclosing transaction as failed: the transaction can report success even though that request failed. The thread's last-sample status, on-error stop actions and logical actions still apply. Scripts that explicitly ignore a result continue to work in every mode.

The selection is saved with the sampler in the test plan and also applies in command-line runs. The control is shared by standard sampler editors and TestBean sampler editors; plugins with fully custom headers may need to adopt the shared title panel to display it. Plugin editors must call super.configure(element) when loading a sampler; otherwise, saving through configureTestElement can write an Ignore setting left over from another sampler.

section.name: Wait for value
section.p: Add the Wait for value action from the sampler menu to coordinate a main branch and its asynchronous forks. It uses the If condition table, including Match all / Match any and the same comparison operators, without a script editor. For example, wait for ${ready} to equal true after a fork sets the ready parameter.
